extracted.intended_audience: criminal lawyers / criminalists / trial judges (practitioners who take and evaluate testimony)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for criminal-law practitioners on how to interpret, elicit, and evaluate oral testimony, focusing on language, dialect, forms of expression, context, and nonverbal cues. Emphasizes reconstructing subjective meaning and the functions of understanding before judging emotional or verbal statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of language and its refinements
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminalist must know language completely and in all its refinements; study the general character, origins, force, nature, and development of language as a first necessity for taking and interpreting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A failure in proper understanding of language may give rise to false conceptions and the most serious of mistakes; there is an exceedingly rich literature available. The lawyer must undertake careful investigation of the essence of language itself because everything perceived must be clothed in words before it can be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of an individual's forms of expression together with character
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person's especial and private forms of expression must be studied in conjunction with their character; 'a man is as he speaks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of modes of expression requires attending to group and individual conditions. Knowing the tricks of speech belonging to an individual gives a clear conception of his character and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of group/corporate speech and slang
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize words and forms that belong to particular corporations, groups, or classes (students, soldiers, hunters, etc.), since use of a single term may place the user in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (student slang 'speer') show how a single term can reveal affiliation; be alert to social variants that could identify or implicate a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine precise meaning of words and abstract terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever anything abstract is named, first determine accurately what the interlocutor means by his word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical or specialist language may have different meanings to speakers; ancient mistakes arose from linguistic classification. Always clarify intended sense before relying on testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for semantic change and substitutions of similars
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to gradual or rapid changes in word meanings and the danger of repeated substitution of similar items producing incommensurability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track how words may have shifted meaning (examples from language history). Repeated substitution (A→B→C...) can end in a substantial drift from the original referent; trace development in individual speakers to avoid misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider influence of time interval on testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The interval between observation and statement affects the form and content of exposition; testimony given immediately may be presented differently than weeks later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mittermaier and Bentham noted the effect of delay; the witness may use different words and concepts later, so compare prior examinations carefully and reconstruct what the witness meant at each time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the effect of audience and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions under which evidence is given (silent office vs. open trial before jury) significantly influence the manner of giving testimony and can alter its presentation though not its essential content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A larger number of attentive hearers can intensify 'reproductive construction' when the speaker is confident, but can also confuse or depress a witness who feels hostility. Account for audience size, attention, and attitude when evaluating changes between earlier and later statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for speaker's tone/manner (humor, melancholy, bitterness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness's humorous, melancholic, or bitter manner can change the perceived seriousness or character of events without any untrue word having been uttered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can reduce perceived danger of a story; melancholy can magnify it. Consider how the narrator's affect may reframe events and influence jurors or judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe non-verbal behavior and gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements of the hands and other gestures while making statements help maintain correct balance; movements lie much less frequently than words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gestures as corroborative cues alongside verbal testimony; they may reveal authenticity or internal coherence of recollection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether witness's causal connections satisfy himself
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe whether the causal relations the witness asserts are 'satisfactory to him'; if they are, his narrative convinces auditors; when they fail, the witness is either lying or uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invert Stricker's observation: as auditors, note if the witness's own causal understanding is coherent—coherence increases credibility, incoherence suggests falsehood or misexpression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn local dialects of populations dealt with
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconditionally know the dialects of those people you most deal with; ignorance of dialects causes great and serious misunderstandings, sometimes irreversible because they begin in the protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning dialects is not hard if one values them; dialects are as living and interesting as literary language. Know common local meanings and idioms to avoid errors in depositions and records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of affected/pretentious speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of uneducated city speakers who use uncomprehended phrases to appear educated; such twisted constructions make it hard to determine what the speaker meant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate genuine unusual forms from mere 'showing off' and probe meaning when forms are twisted or lack purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch dialectal lexical gaps affecting descriptions (e.g., colors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialects can be poorer than literary language in certain domains (e.g., color terms), affecting descriptive testimony—'black' for blue grapes, 'white' for light wine, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take dialectal limitations into account in descriptions of clothes, objects, and colors; seek clarification rather than assume literal equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate individual connotations of foreign and technical words
rubrics_metrics.description: When foreign words or technical terms are adopted, observe the tendency and specific meaning their adoption embodies in that speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign terms may be used to indicate degrees of intensity or nuance; their effect on the native term's meaning is individual and must be examined case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicit direct discourse from uneducated witnesses carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneducated witnesses tend to recall meaning, not exact words; to get exact phrasing ask them to role-play ('Now you are A and I am B; how did it happen?'), but be cautious about reliability of forced direct quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated prompting for actual words can produce extraordinary or unreliable quotations; treat such elicited direct speech with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake silence for guilt or cunning
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence among peasants or country people is common and may be incapacity rather than refractoriness; do not hastily interpret silence as cunning or a sign of guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertain whether silence is natural to the individual; adjust interrogation pace and expectations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat certain uneducated witnesses like children in concept formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneducated individuals and children may not subordinate things under higher concepts and may name new things by old names; their speech is imagistic rather than abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive important material from seemingly worthless statements by discovering intended significance of simple images; avoid trickery and interpret images in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and account for figurative, pictorial, and exaggerated expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many everyday expressions are pictorial or exaggerated (e.g., 'I press through' where nothing physical was pressed); whenever images are used, establish how and where they occurred to know what was meant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe to distinguish literal from figurative use, and trace remoteness between image and referent to avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect euphemisms and social beautifications that minimize wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers often use beautifying language (e.g., 'noble sport') to make misconduct appear more acceptable; such usage can influence legal interpretation and mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize social usages that excuse or favor certain conduct and correct for their mitigating rhetorical effect when assessing culpability and facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist on clear, explicit speech to avoid mutual but different understandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid situations where speaker and hearer each mean different things but assume agreement; open and clear speaking is essential to prevent harmful misunderstandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on assumed concurrence; require explicit statements to ensure both parties refer to the same object or person (e.g., when discussing a suspected criminal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret novel-object references via images and inquire about unfamiliarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a speaker uses an image for an unfamiliar object (e.g., 'wood-dog' for wolf), first learn what was new and foreign to him, then expect imagistic descriptions and decode them accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about the speaker's exposure to the object and anticipate metaphorical naming; use repeated restatement to recover original forms if foreign words are garbled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with abbreviations, contractions, and synthesized titles/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviated or contracted expressions ('old semester', 'From Cliff to Sea') can be unintelligible outside particular groups and require explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query witnesses about shorthand phrases and locally synthesized terms to recover full intended meaning; don't assume literal spatial or semantic sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat circumlocutive or rounded numerical/figurative statements skeptically
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumlocutions ('half-a-dozen' vs. 'six', 'four syllables' vs. 'one') may be used to generalize or aid memory and may not be precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test the reliability of such statements and whether they were chosen for generalization or mnemonic reasons before taking numeric or quantitative claims at face value.
